title: Rigatoni alla Genovese
subtitle: Rigatoni with the Neapolitan slow-cooked onion and beef sauce
excerpt: Rigatoni alla genovese is a Neapolitan dish, not Genoese despite the name: a sauce of beef braised with an enormous quantity of onions for 3 to 4 hours until both break down into a silky, sweet, savoury mass. The beef is served separately as a second course, and the sauce: thick with dissolved onions: is tossed with rigatoni.
sourceNotes: La Genovese is a Neapolitan Sunday dish of disputed origin: most likely named after Genoese merchants or cooks in 15th-century Naples, not the city of Genoa itself. It is documented in Neapolitan cooking from the Renaissance period onward and remains a celebrated dish of Campanian home cooking.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze the sauce (without the beef) for up to 3 months.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: The sauce improves overnight. Make the full braise a day ahead, refrigerate, then reheat gently before tossing with pasta.

glossaryTerms.definition: Cooking meat slowly in a covered pot with a small amount of liquid over a long period, so the collagen breaks down and the meat becomes very tender.

content.text: Rigatoni alla genovese is a Neapolitan dish, not a Genoese one. It is a sauce of beef braised with a large quantity of onions for 3 to 4 hours. Both cook down to a thick, golden sauce. The name has nothing to do with Genoa or pesto. It is believed to refer to Genoese merchants in 15th-century Naples who brought the dish with them.

Warm the olive oil in a large Dutch oven over medium-high heat. Brown the beef all over, 2 to 3 minutes per side. Remove and set aside. Add the prosciutto and cook for 1 minute. Add the carrot and celery and cook for 3 to 4 minutes.

Add all the sliced onions. This will seem like too many: it is not. Stir to coat in the oil. Add the white wine and stir. Nestle the beef piece down into the onions. The onions will eventually subside and surround the beef.

Cover and cook over the lowest possible heat for 3 to 4 hours, checking every 45 minutes and stirring to prevent sticking. The onions will gradually collapse and turn golden and very soft. If the pan dries out, add a small splash of water. Season after 2 hours.
When the onions are golden, thick, and almost jammy, lift out the beef. Taste and adjust seasoning. The sauce should be thick enough to coat the back of a spoon heavily.

Cook the rigatoni in well-salted boiling water until 1 minute short of al dente. Reserve a cup of pasta water, then drain. Toss the rigatoni with the onion sauce over medium heat, adding pasta water to loosen. Finish with a generous amount of Parmigiano Reggiano.
Slice the beef and serve it as a second course with the remaining sauce or alongside a green salad.

items.symptom: Onions catch and burn at the base of the pot
items.cause: Heat too high for the long cook
items.fix: This dish must cook over the absolute lowest heat. Use a heat diffuser if available. Check and stir every 30 to 45 minutes and add a splash of water if the base looks dry.

items.symptom: Sauce is still thin and watery after 3 hours
items.cause: Onions have not broken down fully
items.fix: Remove the lid and cook for another 30 minutes to evaporate the remaining liquid. The onions should look golden and almost paste-like.

items.cause: Temperature was too low and collagen did not break down, or chuck was a very lean cut
items.fix: Continue braising. Chuck needs 3.5 to 4 hours at a steady low simmer to become tender. A lean piece may take longer.

content.text: La genovese is a Neapolitan Sunday tradition going back at least to the 15th century, when merchants from Genoa traded in the city and apparently introduced their cooking. The name stuck even though the dish has no clear counterpart in modern Genoese cooking. In Naples it is a two-course meal in one pot: pasta first, then the braised beef with vegetables. The dish is now experiencing a revival outside Italy through food writers who recognise it as one of the most technically simple and rewarding of the great slow braises.
